verses.text: Dead flies cause the oil of the perfumer to produce an evil odor; so does a little folly outweigh wisdom and honor.
A wise man’s heart is at his right hand, but a fool’s heart at his left.
Yes also, when the fool walks by the way, his understanding fails him, and he says to everyone that he is a fool.
If the spirit of the ruler rises up against you, don’t leave your place; for gentleness lays great offenses to rest.
There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, the sort of error which proceeds from the ruler.
Folly is set in great dignity, and the rich sit in a low place.
I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking like servants on the earth.
He who digs a pit may fall into it; and whoever breaks through a wall may be bitten by a snake.
Whoever carves out stones may be injured by them. Whoever splits wood may be endangered thereby.
If the ax is blunt, and one doesn’t sharpen the edge, then he must use more strength; but skill brings success.
If the snake bites before it is charmed, then is there no profit for the charmer’s tongue.
The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious; but a fool is swallowed by his own lips.
The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness; and the end of his talk is mischievous madness.
A fool also multiplies words. Man doesn’t know what will be; and that which will be after him, who can tell him?
The labor of fools wearies every one of them; for he doesn’t know how to go to the city.
Woe to you, land, when your king is a child, and your princes eat in the morning!
Happy are you, land, when your king is the son of nobles, and your princes eat in due season, for strength, and not for drunkenness!
By slothfulness the roof sinks in; and through idleness of the hands the house leaks.
A feast is made for laughter, and wine makes the life glad; and money is the answer for all things.
Don’t curse the king, no, not in your thoughts; and don’t curse the rich in your bedroom: for a bird of the sky may carry your voice, and that which has wings may tell the matter.

footnotes.content: One small rotting thing spoils what took care to make beautiful. I've seen it in people too—a little carelessness, one unguarded moment, can stain a whole life of good work. But grace still restores; Jesus teaches us that small wrongs don't have to be the end of our story.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wise keep their heart steady and true; the foolish lean toward what's wrong as if drawn by habit. Right and left, heart and path—they belong together. Our walk follows where our heart first decided to go.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A fool's own confusion announces itself—he doesn't hide it, doesn't repent, just walks on declaring his own foolishness. There's something sadly honest in that: we broadcast what we really believe. Thank God His mercy doesn't wait for us to figure it out ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When anger rises in power over us, steadiness—not flight—is the wiser choice. Gentleness quiets great wrongs. Even before kings, the meek find favor. Jesus showed us this: silence before Pilate held more power than any word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Under the sun, we see the wrong person in the wrong place—folly elevated, justice abandoned. It happens, and it grates on the soul. But the sun rises and sets; beyond it, God sees and holds the true weight of things.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The world often puts the least fit in the highest seat and leaves the worthy waiting below. We see it, we taste the injustice. Yet the Lord's kingdom inverts all earthly rank—the last shall be first, the servant greatest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I've watched servants ride high and nobles walk like servants. The outward station lies; what you really are lives inside. God knows who you truly are whether you're on a horse or on foot.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dig a pit for others and you may tumble in yourself; break down what protects you and danger bites back. The harm we intend has a way of returning home. But Jesus breaks that cycle—He bore what we deserved so we wouldn't have to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every tool that does work carries risk; every stone you move or wood you split can hurt you back. We live in a world where labor costs something. Yet when we offer our sweat to God's purpose, He sees it and honors it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A dull blade demands twice the strength for half the result; a sharpened one does more with ease. Life teaches this: we can live in constant strain fighting with dull tools, or we can take time to sharpen—to learn, to prepare, to seek wisdom first. Skill, not just muscle, brings through.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A snake bites before you can charm it; some harms arrive faster than we can respond. We can't prepare for every danger, can't charm our way past every harm. There's a hard truth here—and it drives us to trust something bigger than our own skill.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A wise one's words flavor like grace; a fool's words consume him, swallowed by his own tongue. We become what we speak into being. Jesus knew this—He guarded His words like they were seeds; He calls us to the same care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Foolishness opens a fool's mouth; madness is where it ends. One unwise word leads to another until you can't recognize yourself anymore. Wisdom knows when to speak and when to listen. Blessed are those who grow quiet enough to hear the still, small voice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A fool talks on and on—many, many words—as if noise could fill the void of not knowing. We don't know what comes next; that's where wisdom bows low and asks for guidance. The fool multiplies words; the wise man multiplies listening.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hard labor wears the fool down because he doesn't know the way forward—he thrashes instead of thinking. Even simple tasks become exhausting when done without direction. There's a weariness that comes from refusing to ask for help or seek a better path.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A king who is still a child, princes feasting at dawn—that's a land in trouble. Youth without wisdom, indulgence without restraint, leadership without purpose: these drain a kingdom. A people needs shepherds who shepherd, not children who play.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Blessed is the land whose king is nobly born and whose leaders eat in due season, with strength and not with drunkenness. Maturity, purpose, and self-rule—these are the gifts a leader gives a people. Such blessing comes from character, not accident.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A roof sags from laziness; a house leaks from idle hands. Small neglect becomes big ruin over time. The Lord gives us stewardship—of our homes, our work, ourselves—and invites us to tend it faithfully, not from fear but from love of what He's entrusted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A feast brings laughter, wine glads the heart, money seems to answer everything. But it doesn't—not really. These pleasures are real and good in their place, but they can't fill what only the Lord can fill. Joy without Him is thirst that never quite ends.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo here: even in private chambers, our words carry. A bird hears, a swift bearer spreads the word. We live as if watched—and we are, by the Lord who hears every word. Grace invites us to speak truth even in secret, knowing He already knows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
